dispatches.title: The Blue Food Swap
dispatches.standfirst: The next debt conversion is bound to local farms, fisheries and sea farming.
dispatches.caption: Barbadians moderately or severely food insecure
dispatches.challenge: About 88,000 Barbadians, three in ten, are moderately or severely food insecure.
dispatches.advises: Barbados should make its next debt conversion a blue food swap, refinancing costly debt with guaranteed debt and binding the savings to local farms, fisheries and sea farming, so the island grows more of what it eats. With super intelligence, food prices, harvests and fish stocks can be read week by week, so support reaches the households that cannot count on enough good food before prices rise.
how: A sea many times larger than its land, and two debt conversions already completed.
A debt-for-food conversion: guaranteed debt replaces costly debt; the savings grow local food.
More food grown and caught at home, and fewer families going without.

dispatches.title: The Rift Reading Bond
dispatches.standfirst: Kenyans buy a reading bond by phone, backed by the heat of the Rift.
dispatches.caption: Kenyan children who reach the end of primary school unable to read
dispatches.challenge: Four in five Kenyan children reach the end of primary school unable to read a simple text.
dispatches.advises: Kenya should sell a reading bond to its own citizens by phone, as it did with M-Akiba, back it with part of the revenue from its geothermal power, and release funds to schools as children learn to read. With super intelligence, reading can be assessed in English and Kiswahili on a phone in every school, and every bondholder can see how many children their savings helped to read.
how: Geothermal heat under the Rift, and citizens who already buy bonds by phone.
A retail reading bond, backed in part by geothermal revenue.
Every Kenyan child reading by the end of primary school.

dispatches.title: Solar Schools, Reading Children
dispatches.standfirst: Solar on every government school, and the power savings finance children learning to read.
dispatches.caption: of Indian children could not read a simple text, 2017
dispatches.challenge: 56% of Indian children could not read a simple text by the end of primary school in 2017.
dispatches.advises: India should put solar on the roof of every government school through its sovereign green bonds, and commit the electricity savings to reading programmes rewarded on results, as the Educate Girls impact bond first did in Rajasthan. With super intelligence, every child can have a reading tutor in their own language on a shared device, and every school’s progress and power savings can be seen side by side.
how: Solar at world scale, sovereign green bonds, and schools in every village.
Green bonds for school rooftops; the savings rewarded to schools on reading results.
Children who read, in schools that make their own clean power.

dispatches.title: Every Street Connected
dispatches.standfirst: A sanitation bond whose return rises with every home connected to a safe toilet and sewer.

dispatches.challenge: About 109 million Brazilians, about one in two, have no safely managed toilet at home.
dispatches.advises: Brazil should issue a sanitation outcome bond under its sustainable bond framework, with the return rising as each verified household is connected to a safe toilet and sewer, and pair it with the currency hedging that Eco Invest Brasil already offers foreign investors. With super intelligence, every street without sewerage can be mapped from satellite and census data, so concessions are priced street by street and no community is left until last.
how: A sustainable bond framework that investors trust, and a currency hedge already built.
A sanitation outcome bond, with the return linked to verified connections.
A safe toilet and sewer for every Brazilian home.
dispatches.first: Add sanitation outcomes to the sustainable bond framework and name the first cities.

dispatches.title: Standard Tokens for Clean Kitchens

dispatches.challenge: About 13 million Rwandans, nine in ten, cook without clean fuel or technology.

how: A nation that registers new investment fast, and visitors who care about its hills and forests.
Standard Tokens: citizen-scale units of finance, each tied to one clean kitchen.
A clean kitchen in every home, and forests spared from firewood.

Every child who can be reached, learning to read.

body: The United Republic of Tanzania has signed a US$1.2 billion commercial financing facility for Lot 6 of its Standard Gauge Railway: the 411-kilometre electrified line from Tabora to Kigoma. The African Development Bank (AfDB), acting as Initial Mandated Lead Arranger, structured a partial credit guarantee of up to US$800 million, the largest the Bank has issued to date, according to its release of 4 November 2026.
## What it is

A partial credit guarantee is a promise by a development bank to repay lenders, up to a set amount, if the borrower does not. It lets a sovereign borrow from commercial banks on the strength of the guarantor’s balance sheet as well as its own. This guarantee covers the principal of the covered tranche plus two years of interest, and it is priced on non-market terms.
## Who lends and on what terms

Nine banks make up the syndicate. Deutsche Bank and Société Générale co-arranged it, with HSBC, Commerzbank, Nedbank, Stanbic Bank Tanzania, First Abu Dhabi Bank, FirstBank UK and Bank of Africa United Kingdom. Of the US$1.2 billion, US$720 million is guaranteed lending and US$480 million is lent on clean risk to the sovereign, on Tanzania’s own credit. The release does not state tenor or pricing.

The AfDB remains the guarantor of record, but it does not carry the whole exposure. Credit insurance arranged by the broker Texel places US$405.5 million of it with a panel of international insurers, including Lloyd’s syndicates. Private risk-bearing capacity sits behind a public guarantee, and more commercial lending can follow. The AfDB calls it blended finance in practice.
## What it finances

Lot 6 carries the line west to Lake Tanganyika. Through the lake ports of Kigoma and Kalemie it links the port of Dar es Salaam to trade with eastern DR Congo, with wider links to Burundi. The AfDB expects it to give western Tanzania a long-haul, high-volume route for production and trade, to lower transport costs and to create jobs.

The facility is one part of a US$2.3 billion package for the section. The package also holds an export credit agency tranche and a further tranche to be mobilised with a co-guarantor, under a mandate from Tanzania to the AfDB to structure and mobilise up to US$3.2 billion for its regional railway programme. The syndication began with a coordination letter signed with Deutsche Bank and Société Générale in Rabat in December 2024.
## Which standards it moves

Livelihood first: a cheaper route to the coast and to the lake ports is income for farms, mines and traders far from Dar es Salaam. Food second: the AfDB described the corridor in 2024 as a route for agricultural and mining commodities. The railway does not reach the standard that sets Tanzania’s Coverage. Only 11% of Tanzanians cook with clean fuels and technology.
## Could it work elsewhere

The structure needs three things: a sovereign that commercial banks will lend to, a development bank willing to put its guarantee behind the debt, and insurers willing to share that guarantee. Uganda, where the AfDB tentatively allocated funding to its own standard gauge railway in May 2026, is the nearest test of the same blend.
deals.kick: One guarantee, shared with insurers, has brought nine banks to a railway. The export credit and co-guaranteed tranches will show whether the model carries the rest of the line.

body: The Board of Executive Directors of the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) has approved a US$175 million guarantee for Barbados, with a term of 20 years. The guarantee supports a refinancing of Barbados debt on more favourable terms. The fiscal savings will fund approximately US$160 million of investment through the Health Services Resilience Program, according to the IDB announcement carried on 30 October 2026.
## What it is

A debt-for-health operation is a debt swap whose savings are bound to health. A development bank guarantee lowers the risk that lenders carry, so the new debt costs less than the debt it replaces. The difference does not return to the budget at large: it is committed to a named programme. The approach frees fiscal space without adding new debt. Earlier debt swaps in Barbados and Belize bound the savings to nature and climate; this operation binds them to the health system.
## Who issued it and on what terms

At the request of the Government of Barbados, the IDB led the assembly of a package of guarantees from participating development institutions. The IDB share is US$175 million over 20 years. The other guarantors and their amounts are not named in the IDB announcement.

The operation is the first under the Multi-Guarantor Debt for Resilience Initiative, launched at COP30 in Belém in November 2025 by the IDB, CAF–Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Caribbean Development Bank. Each guarantor keeps its own procedures and approvals, while a regional facility harmonises guarantee terms, climate-resilience taxonomies and performance indicators. Every swap under the initiative must carry a regional public-goods component.
## What it finances

The Health Services Resilience Program targets noncommunicable diseases and mental health. It funds upgraded facilities and services; prevention, early detection and management of chronic illness in primary and community care; interoperable health information systems and telehealth; and infrastructure built to keep care running through climate shocks. Its regional component supports a Caribbean pharmaceutical hub, to make pharmaceutical and medical supplies more dependable across the region.

The Ministry of Health and Wellness held public consultations in August and September 2026 on the sites the programme will touch: the Roseville Halfway House, the Geriatric Hospital Phase II and the National Rehabilitation Centre, the Senior Citizens Villages at Odle’s Glen, the Enmore site for the Queen Elizabeth Hospital, and digital health services.
## Which standard it moves

Health, the sixth of the seven standards. The money does not wait on new borrowing room in the budget. It comes from lowering the cost of debt that Barbados already carries, and it is committed before the savings can be spent on anything else.
## Could it work for another nation

The structure suits a small sovereign with costly debt and a costed public programme ready to absorb the savings. Saint Lucia, a fellow borrowing member of the Caribbean Development Bank, could follow under the same initiative. The framework is regional by design, and the pharmaceutical hub that Barbados is building already offers the kind of regional public good that each new swap must carry.
deals.kick: A guarantee adds no new debt. It changes what the old debt costs, and Barbados has already decided where the difference goes.

body: In June 2026 the Republic of Zambia retired almost all of its US$1.36 billion Eurobond due 2053. Holders of 97.91% of the outstanding principal, US$1,336,149,768, tendered their notes, and Zambia announced that it would redeem the remaining US$28,575,796 by 25 June 2026. The purchase was paid for with a US$600 million loan from the African Development Bank Group and the government’s own resources. In return, the Ministry of Finance and National Planning committed to earmark US$275 million of the savings for the energy sector, to be invested over 15 years.
## What it is

A debt-for-development swap replaces costly or risky debt with cheaper debt and binds part of the difference to a public purpose. Debt-for-nature swaps bind the savings to conservation. Zambia bound them to electricity: the reliability of supply, losses on the distribution network, and access in underserved areas. The African Development Bank Group calls the transaction a global landmark, and Zambia describes it as Africa’s first debt-for-development transaction focused on energy.
## The terms

The 2053 bond was a product of Zambia’s Eurobond restructuring. To buy it back, Zambia ran a cash tender offer, led by Citigroup. When a group of holders resisted, the government raised its price and added a US$65 million payment, and support became near unanimous. Notes tendered after the early deadline were bought at US$740 per US$1,000 of principal, plus accrued interest. Settlement was set for on or around 15 June 2026, or the drawdown of the new loan, whichever came later.

The result is a change of creditor as much as a change of cost. A bond held by private investors became a loan from a development lender, and a share of the saving became a published commitment that can be tracked.
## Which standards it moves

Energy first. Every dollar of the earmark goes to the grid that powers homes, clinics and schools. Livelihood second: a reliable supply is the condition for the mines, farms and small firms that employ Zambians. Health and education follow, because a clinic without power cannot keep vaccines cold and a school without light closes at dusk.
The swap does not by itself reduce what Zambia owes to the world. It replaces one obligation with another on better terms, and it ties the gain to the one standard that carries the others.
## Could it work elsewhere

The structure needs three things: a bond trading below its face value, a development lender willing to refinance it, and a finance ministry willing to name where the savings go. Mozambique is the nearest candidate. It signed an agreement with China on 28 October 2026 to restructure its debt and adjust payment schedules. If its Eurobond due 2031 trades at a discount, a buyback funded by a development bank loan could release savings for water or electricity.
The test for every nation is the same. A discount on a bond is a saving only if it is captured, and a saving is development only if it is spent where it was promised.
deals.kick: Debt that costs less can be made to build more. Zambia has put the saving into the grid and published the number.

body: In March 2026 the Ci Gaba Fund of Funds reached a first close of GHS 383 million in Accra, after five years of design and market-building. It became the first private fund of funds domiciled in West Africa to bring domestic institutional capital, chiefly pension funds, into private markets for small and medium enterprises. More than two-thirds of the commitments came from Ghanaian pension funds. The target is GHS 1 billion.
## What it is

A fund of funds does not lend to businesses. It commits capital to smaller, specialist venture capital, private equity and private debt funds that sit closer to the enterprises they back. Ci Gaba is denominated in Ghanaian cedis, managed by Savannah Impact Advisory and sponsored by Impact Investing Ghana. It invests across Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal and Côte d’Ivoire, in financial services, healthcare, agriculture, clean energy, education and technology. FMO, the Dutch development bank, records that up to 40% of its investments are targeted at enterprises founded or led by women.
## How it was built

The structure is blended. Catalytic investors take the early risk so that pension trustees can invest within their fiduciary duties. FSD Africa Investments committed US$7.5 million, and Small Foundation committed alongside it. FMO supported the fund manager’s operating costs, and grants from the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office through its RISA Fund, GSG Impact, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan and the Argidius Foundation paid for design and set-up. Capital comes paired with technical assistance for fund managers, enterprises and pension trustees.
## Why the currency matters

A pension fund owes its members cedis. A dollar fund adds a currency risk most trustees cannot carry; a cedi fund removes it. That one design choice opens a pool of capital that has mostly sat in government securities. Across Africa, pension funds manage more than US$455 billion, most of it in that same paper.
## Which standards it moves

Livelihood, most directly. The seven basic living standards are food, water, shelter, energy, education, health and livelihood. FSD Africa expects Ci Gaba to support up to 25,000 jobs, while widening pension portfolios beyond government bonds.
## Where it could work next

Any nation whose pension savings are concentrated in its own sovereign debt holds the raw material for a fund like this. Kenya is a natural candidate. The builders of Ci Gaba warn that local trust must be earned first, and that earning it takes years.

body: On 29 June 2026 Ethiopia’s Ministry of Finance announced an agreement in principle with an Ad Hoc Committee of institutional holders controlling approximately 45% of its US$1 billion 6.625% Notes due 2024, the bond on which it defaulted. On 20 August the Ministry published the Official Creditor Committee’s finding, dated 31 July, that the terms comply with the principle of comparability of treatment. In mid-October the exchange was reported to be near; it has not yet been launched.
## What it is

Two securities replace one. The first is a new bond of US$880 million, a 12% haircut to principal, paying 6.15% and maturing on 15 July 2029. The three missed coupons, USD 99.375 million, are paid in full at settlement. The second is new: a New Money Warrant, a separate and tradable right to subscribe for a future Ethiopian international bond of up to USD 1 billion, issued at par, with a 7-year tenor and a coupon of 450 basis points over 6-year U.S. Treasuries. The strike date falls in a one-year window from 1 July 2028. Ethiopia may instead redeem the warrant, at a price capped at 9% of the notional redeemed.
## What it changes

Ethiopia’s first terms, announced in January 2026, compensated bondholders through a value recovery instrument tied to the nation’s exports of goods. The June terms set that aside for a claim on Ethiopia’s return to the market: holders who exercise the warrant become buyers of its next bond. The IMF reviewed the warrant and confirmed it would be consistent with Ethiopia’s debt sustainability targets. The official creditors set one condition in plain terms: if the warrant is used to give bondholders excessive benefits, they will adjust their own debt treatment through proportionate compensation.
## Which standards it moves

None directly. The seven basic living standards are food, water, shelter, energy, education, health and livelihood. Until the exchange closes, the 2024 Notes remain in default. Closing it is the step that opens the way to the Future Eurobond the warrant describes, and to budgets planned on borrowing the nation can count on.
## Where it could work next

Mozambique is the nearest candidate. In its February 2026 Article IV report the IMF classified the nation’s public debt as in distress, with debt service arrears above 1 percent of GDP at end-2025, and found that under current policies it is unsustainable. A nation that must ask its creditors for relief, and will need them again, could offer the same seat at its next bond.
deals.kick: Ethiopia is asking its bondholders to accept less now and lend again later. The warrant turns that promise into a security.
